claim: Cacopsylla chinensis (Yang & Li) showed two seasonal morphotypes, summer-form and winter-form, with significant differences in morphological characteristics.
source: Cacopsylla chinensis (Yang & Li) showed two seasonal morphotypes, summer-form and winter-form, with significant differences in morphological characteristics.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by morphological descriptions and images in Figure 1.

claim: Low temperature is the key environmental factor to induce the transition from summer-form to winter-form in C. chinensis.
source: Low temperature is the key environmental factor to induce its transition from summer-form to winter-form.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through temperature treatment experiments shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Low temperature of 10 °C induced the transition from summer-form to winter-form by affecting the cuticle thickness and chitin content.
source: Here, we firstly confirmed that low temperature of 10 °C induced the transition from summer-form to winter-form by affecting the cuticle thickness and chitin content.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by transmission electron microscopy and chitin content measurements shown in Figure 1H-K.

claim: CcTRPM functions as a temperature receptor to regulate the transition from summer-form to winter-form.
source: Subsequently, we demonstrated that CcTRPM functions as a temperature receptor to regulate this transition.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by calcium imaging experiments, RNAi knockdown experiments, and rescue experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: miR-252 was identified to mediate the expression of CcTRPM to involve in the morphological transition.
source: In addition, miR-252 was identified to mediate the expression of CcTRPM to involve in this morphological transition.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by dual-luciferase reporter assays, RIP assays, and FISH experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: CcTre1 and CcCHS1 act as the critical down-stream signal of CcTRPM in mediating the behavioral transition.
source: Finally, we found CcTre1 and CcCHS1, two rate-limiting enzymes of insect chitin biosyntheis, act as the critical down-stream signal of CcTRPM in mediating this behavioral transition.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by RNAi experiments and expression analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: All the survived treated nymphs develop to the 3rd instar winter-form nymphs at 10 °C.
source: The results indicated that all the survived treated nymphs develop to the 3rd instar summer-form nymphs at 25 °C, approximately 17% and 40% of survived treated nymphs develop to the 3rd instar winter-form nymphs at 20°C and 15°C, but all the survived treated nymphs develop to the 3rd instar winter-form nymphs at 10 °C (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1F with quantitative data from temperature treatment experiments.

claim: About 49% and 37% of the survived treated nymphs develop to the 3rd instar winter-form nymphs after menthol and borneol treatment at 25 °C, respectively.
source: We observed that about 49% and 37% of the survived treated nymphs develop to the 3rd instar winter-form nymphs after menthol and borneol treatment at 25 °C, respectively (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1G with quantitative data from cooling agent treatment experiments.

claim: Cuticle thicknesses of 3rd instar winter-form (about 3.86 μm) were obviously higher than 3rd instar summer-form (about 1.82 μm).
source: The ultrastructure results of transmission electron microscopy assays showed that cuticle thicknesses of 3rd instar winter-form (about 3.86 μm) were obviously higher than 3rd instar summer-form (about 1.82 μm) (Figure 1H and I).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by transmission electron microscopy measurements shown in Figure 1H and I.

claim: Winter-form nymphs exhibited higher chitin level in cuticle compared to the summer-form nymphs.
source: We also found that winter-form nymphs exhibited higher chitin level in cuticle compared to the summer-form nymphs by using the WGA-FITC staining and chitin content determination (Figure 1J and K).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by WGA-FITC staining and chitin content measurements shown in Figure 1J and K.

claim: The ORF of CcTRPM was 4566 bp with a 455 bp 3'UTR and encoded a deduced polypeptide of 1521 amino acids with six transmembrane domains.
source: Sequence analysis displayed that the ORF of CcTRPM was 4566 bp with a 455 bp 3'UTR and encoded a deduced polypeptide of 1521 amino acids with six transmembrane domains.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on sequence analysis of the cloned CcTRPM gene.

claim: The mRNA expression of CcTRPM was obviously induced by 10 °C treatment at 1, 2, 3, 6, and 10 days compared with 25 °C treatment.
source: The results of temperature treatment indicated that the mRNA expression of CcTRPM was obviously induced by 10 °C treatment at 1, 2, 3, 6, and 10 days compared with 25 °C treatment by qRT-PCR (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Menthol treatment with all three concentrations significantly increased the mRNA expression of CcTRPM.
source: qRT-PCR results revealed that menthol treatment with all three concentrations significantly increased the mRNA expression of CcTRPM and antagonist (HY-112430, MedChemExpress, Shanghai, China) treatment with all three concentrations markedly reduced CcTRPM transcription (Figure 2—figure supplement 2G–H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2G.

claim: Both 10 °C and menthol treatment obviously elevated intracellular Ca2+ levels in CcTRPM-expressing cells.
source: The effect of 10 °C and menthol on CcTRPM was further tested using Ca2+ imaging and showed that both 10 °C and menthol treatment obviously elevated intracellular Ca2+ levels in CcTRPM-expressing cells (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2I).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2I.

claim: CcTRPM is a cold-sensitive ion channel activated by 10 °C low temperature and menthol.
source: We therefore concluded that CcTRPM is a cold-sensitive ion channel activated by 10 °C low temperature and menthol.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the Results section and supported by calcium imaging and fluorescence detection experiments shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: CcTRPM mRNA expressed in all determined stages, with the highest expression level in the 1st instar nymph.
source: Temporal expression profiles by qRT-PCR revealed that CcTRPM mRNA expressed in all determined stages, with the highest expression level in the 1st instar nymph, and showed a decreased trend from 2nd instar nymph to adult 1 day (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Feeding of dsCcTRPM reduced the transcription level of CcTRPM by about 61% and 62% compare to dsEGFP feeding at 3 days and 6 days.
source: For the RNAi efficiency under 10 °C condition, feeding of dsCcTRPM reduced the transcription level of CcTRPM by about 61% and 62% compare to dsEGFP feeding at 3 days and 6 days by qRT-PCR (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A), and decreased the CcTRPM-Cy3 signal at 6 days by FISH (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by qRT-PCR and FISH data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A-B.

claim: Cuticle thicknesses (about 1.97 μm) and cuticle chitin content of dsCcTRPM-treated nymphs were markedly lower than dsEGFP-treated nymphs (about 3.71 μm) under 10 °C condition.
source: Both results of cuticle ultrastructure and cuticle chitin content determination showed that cuticle thicknesses (about 1.97 μm) and cuticle chitin content of dsCcTRPM-treated nymphs were markedly lower than dsEGFP-treated nymphs (about 3.71 μm) under 10 °C condition (Figure 2G and H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by transmission electron microscopy and chitin content measurements shown in Figure 2G and H.

claim: dsCcTRPM feeding and CcTRPM antagonist treatment both significantly decreased the transition percent from summer-form to winter-form.
source: Additionally, dsCcTRPM feeding and CcTRPM antagonist treatment both significantly decreased the transition percent from summer-form to winter-form, but menthol feeding only partially rescued the transition percent and morphological phenotype under dsCcTRPM feeding (Figure 2I and J).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data and phenotypic images shown in Figure 2I and J.

claim: CcTRPM functions as an essential molecular signal to modulate the transition from summer-form to winter-form of C. chinensis in response to low temperature.
source: Together, these findings indicated that CcTRPM functions as an essential molecular signal to modulate the transition from summer-form to winter-form of C. chinensis in response to low temperature.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the Results section and supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence including RNAi, antagonist treatment, and rescue experiments.

claim: Four miRNAs (miR-252, miR-5728, PC-3p-173924, and PC-3p-137568) were predicted to have the corresponding target-binding sites with the 3'UTR of CcTRPM.
source: There are four miRNAs (miR-252, miR-5728, PC-3p-173924, and PC-3p-137568) were predicted to have the corresponding target-binding sites with the 3'UTR of CcTRPM (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A based on computational predictions using miRanda and Targetscan.

claim: miR-252 showed the opposite expression patterns with CcTRPM after 25°C and 10°C treatments.
source: miR-252 showed the opposite expression patterns with CcTRPM after 25°C and 10°C treatments (Figures 2B and 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figures 2B and 3B.

claim: The relative luciferase activities were obviously decreased when the agomir-252 and CcTRPM-3'UTR-pmirGLO were cotransfected.
source: The relative luciferase activities were obviously decreased when the agomir-252 and CcTRPM-3'UTR-pmirGLO were cotransfected, while the activity recovered to the control when using the mutated 3'UTR sequence without the binding sites of miR-252 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by dual-luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The transcripts of CcTRPM and miR-252 increased 6.35-fold and 9.21-fold from the agomir-252 feeding nymphs of the Ago-1 antibody-mediated RNA complex compared to an IgG control.
source: An RNA immunoprecipitation assay indicated that the transcripts of CcTRPM and miR-252 increased 6.35-fold and 9.21-fold from the agomir-252 feeding nymphs of the Ago-1 antibody-mediated RNA complex compared to an IgG control, separately (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by RIP assay data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: CcTRPM and miR-252 were co-expressed in the nymphs and displayed an opposite expression trend along with the increasing instar.
source: FISH results showed that CcTRPM and miR-252 were co-expressed in the nymphs and displayed an opposite expression trend along with the increasing instar (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by FISH imaging data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Agomir-252 feeding significantly inhibited CcTRPM mRNA expression and antagomir-252 feeding markedly increased CcTRPM mRNA expression.
source: qRT-PCR results indicated that agomir-252 feeding significantly inhibited CcTRPM mRNA expression and antagomir-252 feeding markedly increased CcTRPM mRNA expression compare to their controls, separately (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: miR-252 directly targeted CcTRPM.
source: These data together confirmed that miR-252 directly targeted CcTRPM.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the Results section and supported by multiple experimental approaches including dual-luciferase assays, RIP assays, FISH, and qRT-PCR.

claim: miR-252 expression was both significantly increased after agomir-252 treatment at 3 days and 6 days.
source: qRT-PCR results showed that miR-252 expression was both significantly increased after agomir-252 treatment at 3 days and 6 days (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: miR-252 expression was dramatically inhibited after successful interference of CcTRPM at 3 days and 6 days.
source: Interestingly, miR-252 expression was dramatically inhibited after successful interference of CcTRPM at 3 days and 6 days (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Up-regulation of CcTRPM expression may have a positive feedback to miR-252 expression in response to 10 °C temperature.
source: This result implied that up-regulation of CcTRPM expression may have a positive feedback to miR-252 expression in response to 10 °C temperature.
evidence: This interpretation is stated in the Results section based on the observation that CcTRPM knockdown decreased miR-252 expression.

claim: Cuticle thickness of agomir-252 treated nymphs (about 1.85 μm) was markedly lower than agomir-NC treated nymphs (about 3.70 μm).
source: Results of cuticle ultrastructure indicated that cuticle thickness of agomir-252 treated nymphs (about 1.85 μm) was markedly lower than agomir-NC treated nymphs (about 3.70 μm) (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by transmission electron microscopy measurements shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: Cuticle chitin content of agomir-252 treated nymphs were obviously lower than agomir-NC treated nymphs.
source: Both WAG-FITC staining and chitin content determination revealed that cuticle chitin content of agomir-252 treated nymphs were obviously lower than agomir-NC treated nymphs (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by WGA-FITC staining and chitin content measurements shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: Agomir-252 feeding significantly decreased the transition percent from summer-form to winter-form.
source: Moreover, agomir-252 feeding significantly decreased the transition percent from summer-form to winter-form, but antagomir-252 feeding rescued the defect of transition percent and morphological phenotype under dsCcTRPM treatment (Figure 4G-H, Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data and phenotypic images shown in Figure 4G-H.

claim: miR-252 mediated the transition from summer-form to winter-form in C. chinensis by suppressing CcTRPM via affecting the cuticle thickness and cuticle chitin content.
source: Above all, these results displayed that miR-252 mediated the transition from summer-form to winter-form in C. chinensis by suppressing CcTRPM via affecting the cuticle thickness and cuticle chitin content.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the Results section and supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence including agomir/antagomir treatments, cuticle measurements, and rescue experiments.

claim: A total of 14 transcripts corresponding to 8 genes involved in chitin biosyntheis were identified in C. chinensis.
source: To demonstrate this hypothesis, a total of 14 transcripts corresponding to 8 genes involved in chitin biosyntheis were identified in C. chinensis, with several genes were present in two or more paralogous forms (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The expression of 13 transcripts exhibited overall up-regulation under 10 °C condition at 3 days, 6 days, and 10 days compared to those under 25 °C condition, while levels for CcUAP2 were almost unchanged.
source: Based on the relative gene expression in the heat map, we found that the expression of 13 transcripts exhibited overall up-regulation under 10 °C condition at 3 days, 6 days, and 10 days compared to those under 25 °C condition, while levels for CcUAP2 were almost unchanged (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by qRT-PCR data shown in the heat map in Figure 5B.

claim: Only knockdown of CcTre1 and CcCHS1 obviously decreased the transition percent from summer-form to winter-form.
source: Compared with dsEGFP feeding control, only knockdown of CcTre1 and CcCHS1 obviously decreased the transition percent from summer-form to winter-form, but not by knockdown of the remaining transcripts (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by RNAi screening data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Knockdown of CcTre1 and CcCHS1 markedly reduced the cuticle thickness and cuticle chitin content.
source: Compared with dsEGFP feeding control, knockdown of CcTre1 and CcCHS1 markedly reduced the cuticle thickness and cuticle chitin content (Figure 5D–F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–D,), which were similar with dsCcTRPM feeding and agomir-252 treatment.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by cuticle measurements shown in Figure 5D-F.

claim: CcTRPM knockdown and agomir-252 feeding were both obviously reduced the mRNA expression of CcTre1 and CcCHS1 at 3 days and 6 days.
source: qRT-PCR results indicated that CcTRPM knockdown and agomir-252 feeding were both obviously reduced the mRNA expression of CcTre1 and CcCHS1 at 3 days and 6 days, respectively (Figure 5G–J).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5G-J.

claim: Chitin biosynthesis signaling involved in the transition from summer-form to winter-summer of C. chinensis in response to low temperature and CcTRPM.
source: These phenotypic and molecular data suggested that chitin biosynthesis signaling involved in the transition from summer-form to winter-summer of C. chinensis in response to low temperature and CcTRPM.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the Results section and supported by RNAi experiments and expression analysis of chitin biosynthesis genes.

claim: Insect polyphenism is the phenomenon allows them within a given genotype to produce two or more distinct phenotypes under the challenges posed by environmental variability via beneficial shifts in morphology, behavior, or physiology.
source: Insect polyphenism is the phenomenon allows them within a given genotype to produce two or more distinct phenotypes under the challenges posed by environmental variability via beneficial shifts in morphology, behavior, or physiology (Cridge et al., 2015).
evidence: This definition is stated in the Introduction and supported by a citation to Cridge et al., 2015.

claim: Polyphenism is commonly observed in many insect species, for examples: the solitary and gregarious phases of Locusta migratoria, the short-winged and long-winged morph of Nilaparvata lugens, the wingless and winged aphid of Acyrthosiphon pisum, and the catkin and twig morphs in caterpillars of the moth Nemoria arizonaria.
source: Polyphenism is commonly observed in many insect species, for examples: the solitary and gregarious phases of Locusta migratoria (Ma et al., 2011), the short-winged and long-winged morph of Nilaparvata lugens (Xu et al., 2015), the wingless and winged aphid of Acyrthosiphon pisum (Vellichirammal et al., 2017), and the catkin and twig morphs in caterpillars of the moth Nemoria arizonaria (Simpson et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: C. chinensis belongs to Hemiptera: Psyllidae, which exclusively feeds on pear trees.
source: C. chinensis, belongs to Hemiptera: Psyllidae, which exclusively feeds on pear trees, harms the young shoots and leaves with adult and nymph, and secretes a large amount of honey dew to breed coal pollution bacteria of Gloeodes pomigena (Wei et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by a citation to Wei et al., 2020.

claim: C. chinensis is an important vector of the destructive disease of pear trees, Erwinia amovora.
source: It is also an important vector of the destructive disease of pear trees, Erwinia amovora, and currently one of the key pests in the major pear production areas in many East Asian countries, including China and Japan (Hildebrand et al., 2000; Ge et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to Hildebrand et al., 2000 and Ge et al., 2019.

claim: In most pear production areas of China, the summer-form of C. chinensis are usually present from April to September, whereas winter-form of C. chinensis are present during the rest of the year.
source: In most pear production areas of China, the summer-form of C. chinensis are usually present from April to September, whereas winter-form of C. chinensis are present during the rest of the year (Ge et al., 2019; Wei et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to Ge et al., 2019 and Wei et al., 2020.

claim: The summer-form has lighter body color and stronger activity ability, and causes more serious damage compare with winter-form.
source: The summer-form has lighter body color and stronger activity ability, and causes more serious damage compare with winter-form.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as a description of the biological characteristics of C. chinensis.

claim: The winter-form has brown to dark brown body color and larger body size, but has the weaker activity ability and stronger resistance ability compare with summer-form.
source: The winter-form has brown to dark brown body color and larger body size, but has the weaker activity ability and stronger resistance ability compare with summer-form.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as a description of the biological characteristics of C. chinensis.

claim: The seasonal polyphenism of summer-form and winter-form in C. chinensis could be induced by low temperature and short day.
source: The seasonal polyphenism of summer-form and winter-form in C. chinensis has been recognized for many years and could be induced by low temperature and short day (Oldfield, 1970; Tougeron et al., 2021), but until recently no molecular mechanism had been advanced.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to Oldfield, 1970 and Tougeron et al., 2021.

claim: TRPM8, a member of the TRP family, has been reported as the principal sensor of environmental cold in mammals.
source: TRPM8, a member of the TRP family, has been reported as the principal sensor of environmental cold in mammals (Peier et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by a citation to Peier et al., 2002.

claim: Insects have an evolutionarily conserved TRPM gene which is homologous to mammalian temperature receptor of TRPM8.
source: As a kind of poikilothermic animals, insects also have an evolutionarily conserved TRPM gene which is homologous to mammalian temperature receptor of TRPM8 (Venkatachalam and Montell, 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by a citation to Venkatachalam and Montell, 2007.

claim: Insect cuticle serves as a protective barrier and plays significant roles in supporting the body, resisting the adverse environmental conditions, preventing predators from predation, and preventing pathogens from invading.
source: Insect cuticle serves as a protective barrier and plays significant roles in supporting the body, resisting the adverse environmental conditions, preventing predators from predation, and preventing pathogens from invading (Evans and Sanson, 2005; Vargas et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations to Evans and Sanson, 2005 and Vargas et al., 2014.

claim: Chitin as an extremely important structural component of insects and represents up to 60% of the dry weight in some species.
source: Chitin as an extremely important structural component of insects and represents up to 60% of the dry weight in some species (Richards, 1978).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by a citation to Richards, 1978.

claim: The de novo biosynthesis of chitin has eight enzymatic steps, including 1 Trehalose, 2 enzymes in Glycolysis, 4 enzymes in Hexosamine pathway, and 1 Chitin synthesis.
source: The de novo biosynthesis of chitin has eight enzymatic steps, including 1 Trehalose, 2 enzymes in Glycolysis, 4 enzymes in Hexosamine pathway, and 1 Chitin synthesis (Doucet and Retnakaran, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by a citation to Doucet and Retnakaran, 2012.

claim: The GenBank accession number of CcTRPM was OQ658558.
source: The GenBank accession number of CcTRPM was OQ658558.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section as a factual record of the sequence submission.

claim: Eggs of summer-form are milky white at the initial stage and gradually become yellow white at the later stage.
source: Eggs are long oval shape with a thin tip and a blunt end. Eggs of summer-form are milky white at the initial stage and gradually become yellow white at the later stage (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Eggs of winter-form are mostly yellowish brown or orange.
source: Eggs of winter-form are mostly yellowish brown or orange (Figure 1A').
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1A'.

claim: The 1st instar nymph of summer-form is light yellow and transparent.
source: The 1st instar nymph of summer-form is light yellow and transparent (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The 3rd and 5th instar nymphs of summer-form are yellow-green or blue-yellow, and the wing buds are oblong, protruding and sticking to both sides of the body.
source: The 3rd and 5th instar nymphs of summer-form are yellow-green or blue-yellow, and the wing buds are oblong, protruding and sticking to both sides of the body (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: The 1st instar nymph of winter-form has many black stripes on the chest back plate, and the end of the abdomen and back are black.
source: The 1st instar nymph of winter-form has many black stripes on the chest back plate, and the end of the abdomen and back are black (Figure 1B').
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1B'.

claim: The 3rd and 5th instar nymphs of winter-form are overall black brown, with dark brown stripe on the left and right sides of each section on the chest and back of the abdomen, and the end of the abdomen and back becomes a large piece with black brown color.
source: The 3rd and 5th instar nymphs of winter-form are overall black brown, with dark brown stripe on the left and right sides of each section on the chest and back of the abdomen, and the end of the abdomen and back becomes a large piece with black brown color (Figure 1C' , and D').
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1C' and D'.

claim: The body color of summer-form adult is green or yellow-green with yellow-brown stripes on the shield of the chest and back plate, and no stripes on the wings.
source: The body color of summer-form adult is green or yellow-green with yellow-brown stripes on the shield of the chest and back plate, and no stripes on the wings (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The body color of winter-form adult is brown or dark brown, with dark brown stripes on the whole body, and clearly brown stripes on the rear edges of the front wings.
source: The body color of winter-form adult is brown or dark brown, with dark brown stripes on the whole body, and clearly brown stripes on the rear edges of the front wings (Figure 1E').
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1E'.

claim: CcTRPM was most closely related to the DcTRPM homologue (Diaphorina citri, XP_017299512.2) in evolutionary relationship.
source: CcTRPM was most closely related to the DcTRPM homologue (Diaphorina citri, XP_017299512.2) in evolutionary relationship, and both of them belong to important Hemiptera pests of fruit trees.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: TRPV ion channel has been reported to function as a heat-activated receptor in mammals by David Julius.
source: TRPV ion channel has been reported to function as a heat-activated receptor in mammals by David Julius (Caterina et al., 1997; Cao et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations to Caterina et al., 1997 and Cao et al., 2013.

claim: miR-34 and miR-9b mediated the wing dimorphism of N. lugens and A. citricidus.
source: For example, miR-34 and miR-9b mediated the wing dimorphism of N. lugens (Ye et al., 2019) and A. citricidus (Shang et al., 2020), miR-133 inhibited behavioral aggregation by controlling dopamine synthesis in L. migratoria (Yang et al., 2014), and miR-31–5 p via asc-C9 to regulate cold acclimation in Monochamus alternatus (Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations to Ye et al., 2019 and Shang et al., 2020.

claim: miR-133 inhibited behavioral aggregation by controlling dopamine synthesis in L. migratoria.
source: For example, miR-34 and miR-9b mediated the wing dimorphism of N. lugens (Ye et al., 2019) and A. citricidus (Shang et al., 2020), miR-133 inhibited behavioral aggregation by controlling dopamine synthesis in L. migratoria (Yang et al., 2014), and miR-31–5 p via asc-C9 to regulate cold acclimation in Monochamus alternatus (Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2014.

claim: miR-31–5 p via asc-C9 to regulate cold acclimation in Monochamus alternatus.
source: For example, miR-34 and miR-9b mediated the wing dimorphism of N. lugens (Ye et al., 2019) and A. citricidus (Shang et al., 2020), miR-133 inhibited behavioral aggregation by controlling dopamine synthesis in L. migratoria (Yang et al., 2014), and miR-31–5 p via asc-C9 to regulate cold acclimation in Monochamus alternatus (Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2020.

claim: In Daphnia pulex, miR-252 might increase cadmium tolerance by switching cellular growth and cuticle protein pathways to detoxification processes.
source: Similar result was reported in Daphnia pulex, miR-252 might increase cadmium tolerance by switching cellular growth and cuticle protein pathways to detoxification processes (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2016.

claim: In Leptinotarsa decemlineata, 42 differentially expressed miRNAs were identified following cold exposure including miR-9a-3p, miR-210–3 p, miR-276–5 p and miR-277–3 p.
source: In Leptinotarsa decemlineata, 42 differentially expressed miRNAs were identified following cold exposure including miR-9a-3p, miR-210–3 p, miR-276–5 p and miR-277–3 p (Morin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by a citation to Morin et al., 2017.

claim: The cricket of Allonemobius socius exhibited darker cuticles to improve thermo-regulation in colder environments.
source: Several similar phenotype changes have been reported in other insects: the cricket of Allonemobius socius exhibited darker cuticles to improve thermo-regulation in colder environments (Fedorka et al., 2013), the mosquito of Aedes albopictus increased the thickness of the egg middle serosa cuticle and wax layer as an adaptation strategy for cold acclimation (Kreß et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by a citation to Fedorka et al., 2013.

claim: The mosquito of Aedes albopictus increased the thickness of the egg middle serosa cuticle and wax layer as an adaptation strategy for cold acclimation.
source: Several similar phenotype changes have been reported in other insects: the cricket of Allonemobius socius exhibited darker cuticles to improve thermo-regulation in colder environments (Fedorka et al., 2013), the mosquito of Aedes albopictus increased the thickness of the egg middle serosa cuticle and wax layer as an adaptation strategy for cold acclimation (Kreß et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by a citation to Kreß et al., 2016.
